Wall Street set a record on Thursday that points to real stress in the stock market. Put volume at Cboe reached 11.23 million contracts on November 5, exceeding the previous record of 10.22 million set on April 4, 2025. That is an increase of approximately 10%. The record came during a selloff that wiped out the post-midterm rally and sent the market's fear index close to its spring highs. It matters now because it shows how fast confidence in the AI-driven bull market turned into a scramble for protection.

Spencer Platt / Getty Images
Record Put Volume Caps a Year of Heavy Hedging

A put option gives its buyer the right to sell a stock or index at a set price before a set date. Investors buy puts to profit from declines or, more often, to protect their portfolios against them, and a spike in put volume shows that many investors are trying to lock in downside protection at the same time.

Thursday's reading continues a longer trend. The 20-day average of put volume has rose to roughly 7 million contracts, compared with approximately 4 million in 2022. That is a 75% increase in average daily activity. Eight of the 10 highest daily put-volume readings reportedly occurred this year, so the rise in hedging goes well beyond one volatile session. Bloomberg reported that options volumes overall hit record levels during the post-election selloff.

PeopleImages / Shutterstock.com

"ETF volume is a fear gauge as big boy traders use them to tweak ports in crisis, and today was a five-alarm fire-type selloff. We were prob due tbh."

Fear Gauges Flashed Red Together

The official fear gauge agreed. The CBOE Volatility Index closed at 28.18 on November 5, up from 16.61 the day before, a 69.7% one-day jump. That was the highest close of the past month and is just under the 30 level that usually marks high fear.

What These Two Funds Actually Own

QQQ seeks to track the Nasdaq-100 Index, which covers 100 of the largest domestic and international non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq. Balchunas wrote that the fund is "27 years old." As of June 30, 2026, it held $490.1 billion in net assets. Its biggest positions were NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) at 7.6%, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) at 6.67%, and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) at 5.64%. The Nasdaq-heavy QQQ has dropped about 13% in a month, while the Dow ETF DIA slid under 1% after the election.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Voters handed Democrats both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterms, so President Donald Trump will govern with a divided Congress starting in January 2027. Wall Street liked the result at first: the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year the next day. Then the mood turned. The tech-heavy index plunged 5.56% on November 5 as investors began pricing in tighter regulation of AI infrastructure. The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, rose to 28.18 from 16.61 a session earlier.

drnadig / iStock via Getty Images

That swing raises a question for investors. Eighty years of midterm history point to a good year ahead for stocks. This cycle could still test that record because so much of the market now rides on one theme.

A Post-Midterm Winning Streak That Has Never Broken

The S&P 500 has risen in all 20 completed 12-month periods after midterm elections since 1946, gaining 14.7% on average. Divided government barely changes that. In 16 of the 21 midterms since 1946, voters sent the president a Congress controlled by the other party. The average 12-month return was 14.6% under divided government and 14.9% under unified government.

Today's setup has the best record of all. The nine instances of a Democratic Congress combined with a Republican president produced an average S&P 500 gain of 16.2% over the following year. Gridlock means fewer policy shocks, a point Reuters reported traders were cheering right after the results.

Average households have started using a phrase once reserved for professional traders. The University of Michigan released its preliminary November 2026 consumer survey on November 6, 2026. It found comments showing what survey director Joanne Hsu called "growing anxiety over a possible AI bubble."

Zanuck from Getty Images and TheaDesign from Getty Images

The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment rose to 51.0 from 48.0 in October. That 6.3% gain only brought it back to the November 2025 reading of 51.0.

Consumers with the most money in stocks moved the other way. Their sentiment fell 5%, while lower- and middle-wealth households became more upbeat.

That split matters if you own the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which closed November 6 at $656.10, up 1.4%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) closed at $735.36, up 0.32%. Over the past month, though, QQQ fell 13.41% while SPY fell 5.39%.

Big Stockholders Soured While Everyone Else Improved

Hsu said most of the small increases in expected personal finances and business conditions came from political independents. The current conditions index rose to 51.0 from 46.7, and expectations rose to 50.9 from 48.8.

The AI-bubble finding comes from open-ended comments, and the survey attached no percentage to it, showing the idea has reached average households but not how many people hold it.

Part of our series on building a mix that lasts. Start here: is 60/40 dead?

Which is real? Both, and the gap between them is the interesting part. In dollars, your S&P 500 fund rose about three-quarters in three years. Measured against gold, it lost ground, because gold did even better. We'll go stock by stock through the biggest names to see who really beat it. Here's what the pros are actually working on, though: not which ruler is right, but what share of their money would hold its value if the dollar keeps losing ground to hard assets. We'll come back to that, with a rule you can set this weekend.

What Does Everyone Already Know?

That stocks have had a great run. Our price data shows the S&P 500 fund SPY up 75.0% over three years, with dividends, from the close on November 6, 2023, to Friday's close.

What fewer people notice is that gold did better. Over the same three years, the gold fund GLD rose about 103%. Divide one by the other and the S&P 500, priced in ounces of gold, fell about 14%.

So Which Number Is Real?

Your bills are in dollars, so the dollar number is the one you live on. If your $100,000 became about $175,000, you can spend $175,000. That's real.

The gold number answers a different question: how much of that gain came from the companies, and how much from the dollar itself buying less? Gold doesn't earn anything, and nobody can print more of it. When stocks beat gold, the businesses outran the currency. When gold beats stocks, part of what looked like growth was the measuring stick shrinking. Over the last three years, by this measure, the stick shrank faster than the average business grew.

A simple way to see it on your own statement: take your balance three years ago and today, and divide each by the gold price on those dates. If the number of ounces went down, your money grew in dollars but lost ground against a hard asset. That doesn't mean you lost money; your groceries are still priced in dollars. It means your plan has been quietly riding on the dollar.

What Does Everyone Already Know?

That bonds have been the boring half of 60/40 for a long time, and in 2022 they were worse than boring. title: What If You Add Gold And Cash To A Dividend Portfolio?

Part of our series on building a mix that lasts. Start here: is 60/40 dead?

Here's the short answer. In the nine and a half years we tested, adding gold and cash to a dividend-and-index portfolio gave you more return than 60/40 and a much smaller loss in 2022, the year bonds let everyone down. We'll show you exactly where that came from, piece by piece. But the more useful question is a quieter one: how many different kinds of bad year can your money survive, and how much are you paying for that insurance? We'll come back to that, with a number you can write down this weekend.

"Cash feels safe. After inflation, it often isn't." - Anonymous

What Does Everyone Already Know?

That 60/40, six parts stocks to four parts bonds, is the plan a lot of retirement money runs on. This series starts from its one blind spot: it works in a growth scare like 2008 and fails in an inflation scare like 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together.

Everyone also knows the usual reputations. Gold is the thing your uncle keeps for the end of the world. Cash is what you hold when you're scared. Dividend stocks are for retirees. Each of those is half true, and the half that's true is exactly why they can be useful together.

So What Happens When You Add Gold And Cash?

We ran the mixes from April 2017 to October 2026, rebalanced every month. The "S&P" part of each mix is the S&P 500 fund (SPY), standing in for a growth sleeve. The "Income" part is the Trefis Income Solution model, before fees. Gold is GLD, cash is the T-bill fund BIL, bonds are AGG.

In dollars, on $100,000, that 2022 gap is the difference between a loss of about $15,800 and a loss of about $6,200. That's the year a lot of people changed their plans at the worst moment, and the smaller number is far easier to sit through.

Is It The Gold And Cash, Or The Dividends?

Fair question, because the dividend sleeve did a lot of the lifting: the Income Solution model was up 2.9% in 2022 while the S&P 500 fell 18.2%. So compare rows three and four of the table. Same 40 Income and 40 S&P; the only change is the last 20%. With bonds there, the mix earned 11.5% a year and lost 8.9% in 2022. With gold and cash, 12.8% and 6.2%. So about 1.3 points a year, and about 2.7 points of the 2022 cushion, came from gold and cash doing what bonds couldn't.

Part of our series on building a mix that lasts. Start here: is 60/40 dead?

Are dividends the new bonds? It's a fair thing to wonder, especially after 2022, when the bond fund lost 13% and a lot of dividend stocks didn't. We'll take it seriously and compare the two honestly: what each pays, whether the payout is safe, taxes and the worst falls. But here's what the question really comes down to for a long-run investor: not which one is better, but which part of your plan each one belongs in. We'll come back to that, and to one comparison worth doing this week.

What Does Everyone Already Know?

A bond pays a fixed coupon and, if the issuer is sound, your money back at the end. A dividend is different in kind. The board decides it, it isn't a contract, and it can be raised, held or cut. The companies with the best records treat that promise very seriously, and some have kept it for decades.

And everyone remembers 2022. Stocks (SPY) fell 18.2% and bonds (AGG) fell 13.0%, the only year since 2004 when both lost money. That year made a lot of people ask whether bonds still do their job, and it is the question this series starts from.

Which Pays More, Dividends Or Bonds?

Today, bonds. Here's what each source of income pays now, and what its income did over the last few years:

Bonds pay more today. A bond fund's income isn't fixed either; it follows rates, both ways.

That middle row surprises people. AGG's payout per share fell from about $3.04 in 2019 to $2.02 in 2021 as rates fell, then climbed back to $3.89 in 2025 as rates rose. A single Treasury held to maturity locks in its coupon. A bond fund doesn't.

Here's a number the pros are watching: the S&P 500's earnings yield is now about 4.4%, below the 10-year Treasury's 4.86%. In 2021 stocks out-yielded the Treasury by 2.63 points; now the gap is about 0.4 point in bonds' favour. Bonds pay well today, and that's worth saying plainly.
